opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to remembering why I started in the first place. When I began working on things like XGBoost or TVM, there wasn't a grand plan. It was really curiosity, and a sense that there was a problem that felt important and that I could actually do something about. That feeling is very easy to lose over time, especially as projects grow, as you take on more responsibilities, and as people start to have expectations of you.

One thing that helps me is to keep treating myself as a student. Even now, I try to stay close to the actual building, writing code, running experiments, talking directly with the students and engineers who are in the trenches. When you stay close to the real problems, you keep getting surprised, and that sense of surprise is what keeps the courage alive. If you only operate from a distance, it's easy to become cautious and to start protecting what you've already done rather than exploring what's next.

Another part is being comfortable with the possibility of failure. A lot of the things I've worked on looked a bit strange or unnecessary at the beginning. People asked, why build a new compiler stack, why care so much about systems when the exciting part is the models? If I had needed everyone's approval first, I probably wouldn't have done them. So I try to remind myself that it's okay if something doesn't work out, as long as I learn something real from it.

And finally, community matters a lot. Open source has been a huge source of energy for me. When you see someone across the world using something you built, contributing back, pushing it in directions you never imagined, it gives you a kind of motivation that's very different from personal achievement. It reminds you that the work is bigger than yourself. That makes it easier to keep going with the same spirit, because you're not just doing it for you, you're doing it alongside a lot of other people who care about the same things.

r001.rationale: The response says the original sense of purpose can be lost over time and that operating at a distance makes it easy to become cautious; it also describes remembering why one started as helpful.

r002.rationale: The response describes remembering the original motivation, but does not frame sustained courage as honoring a commitment made by one’s past self.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because the honest answer is that courage isn't something you preserve in a jar. It drains, and you have to keep refilling it.

For me, the refill comes from a few places. The first is staying close to the problem itself rather than the status of the problem. When I was working on XGBoost, nobody cared about gradient boosting as a "hot" area. It was fun because the math was clean and the engineering was hard. When I started TVM, compilers for machine learning weren't a thing people got excited about either. If I had been chasing what was fashionable, I would have burned out quickly, because fashion moves faster than anyone can build. But if the thing you're working on is intrinsically interesting to you, the motivation is renewable. You wake up and you still want to know the answer.

The second is community. Every project I've been part of that lasted was really a group of people who shared a belief that something should exist and didn't yet. When you have doubts, and you will, someone else in the group doesn't have them that day, and that carries you. Open source has been incredibly important to me for that reason. It's not only a distribution model. It's a way of finding the people who care about the same strange thing you care about.

The third thing, and maybe the most practical one, is to keep the loop short. Big ambitions are fine, but you need something you can finish this week. A benchmark that gets faster. A bug that gets fixed. A student who understands something they didn't yesterday. Courage for the long game is really just the accumulation of small evidence that progress is possible. If you go six months without any of that evidence, no amount of willpower will save you.

And then I'd say, accept that the spirit changes shape. The version of me who wrote XGBoost as a grad student was reckless in ways I can't be anymore, and that's fine. What I try to keep isn't the recklessness, it's the willingness to work on something before it's obvious it will matter. If I can still do that, even in a more careful way, I think the spirit is intact.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the spirit changes shape and values retaining willingness to work before success is obvious, but does not say that people become overly cautious without deliberate reminders to preserve their original aspiration.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses sustaining courage through interest, community, short progress loops, and a continued willingness to take on uncertain work; it does not frame this as honoring a commitment made by one’s past self.

astra-6.text:
I think courage doesn’t mean you always feel confident. Sometimes it just means being willing to take the next step when you don’t know whether something will work. If you need certainty before you begin, it’s very hard to keep going.

For me, it helps to come back to curiosity: Why did I find this problem interesting? Is there still something here that I want to understand? That gives you a reason to continue even when progress is slow. And keeping that spirit doesn’t necessarily mean staying on the same path. You can change your approach and still care about the same question.

The people around you matter, too. Being able to share doubts, explore an idea together, and get excited about a small result makes courage feel less like something you have to maintain alone.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty, curiosity, and support, but does not say that people become more cautious over time without deliberate reminders of their original aspiration.

r002.rationale: The response does not frame courage as honoring a commitment made by one’s past self.

sol-6.1.text:
I think, for me, courage doesn’t mean that you always feel confident about what you’re doing. Often you don’t know whether something will work. But if you’re still curious about the question, you can take a small step, learn something, and then decide what to do next.

It also helps to be around people who are willing to explore with you. When you get stuck, a conversation can remind you why the problem was interesting in the first place. So I wouldn’t say it’s about preserving exactly the same spirit forever. Your interests and your understanding will change. What I hope to preserve is the willingness to try something I don’t yet know how to do, and to be honest when it doesn’t work.

r001.rationale: The response mentions curiosity, small steps, and support from others, but does not say that people become overly cautious without deliberate reminders of their original aspiration.

r002.rationale: The response describes willingness to try as something to preserve, but does not frame courage as honoring a commitment made by one’s past self.
